blocks.text: But let your care go into the air, like a cockchafer that has its foot tied with thread. There again the Scholiast says much the same as you read above. Julius Pollux and Suidas describe the same animal in much the same way. The former says that some write μηλολάνθην [mēlolanthēn] for μηλολόνθη [mēlolonthē] (rather μηλάνθην [mēlanthēn]), ἤτοι ἐκ τῆς ἀνθήσεως τῶν μήλων [ētoi ek tēs anthēseōs tōn mēlōn] (read μηλεῶν [mēleōn] with Eustathius) ἢ σὺν τῇ ἀνθήσει γιγνόμενον [ē syn tē anthēsei gignomenon], either from the blossoms of apple trees, on which Suidas reports that it settles, or because it is born together with the blossoms. If you take all this together, you will at once conclude that the little animal described is one far too well known to us Normans, to our very great harm: for every third year this pest grows worse on the blossoms of the apple trees, from which our most abundant produce comes ^{(1)}. But I see no reason why ילק jelek should be thought to be the melolontha [cockchafer] rather than a kind of bruchus or locust. So all the ancients consistently render it, having been so taught by the Prophets themselves, who in many places of Scripture mention the jelek among the kinds of locusts. For examples see Psal. CV, 34. Ioel. I, 4. and II, 25. and Nahum III, 15. 16. One should therefore not lightly depart from this rendering. Indeed, even if it were granted (it is not conceded) that the jelek is the melolontha, the question posed, why the jelek is described as ὀρθόθριξ [orthothrix], would be solved no more easily. For the melolontha is no less smooth than the locust or the bruchus. Fuller, it is true, who on this point sides with Junius and Tremellius in his Miscellanea, book 5, chapter 9, imagines that a cockchafer flying toward us, with the constant and rapid beating of its four wings, presents the appearance of a hedgehog [col. 456] bristling with spines standing out on every side.
[III, 273] Are we to believe it? Or do those who love invent dreams for themselves?

I, at any rate, do not see what soft wings, blunt at their tips, have in common with the spines of a hedgehog. And even if this were true, it would have been no reason for the recent translators to depart from the accepted rendering, since locusts and bruchi also have four wings, whose beating is as rapid as that of the cockchafer's wings. It would therefore have been just as easy to imagine the very same thing of locusts ^{(2)}.

But to solve the question, there are two things we may answer. 1. It is not certainly established, as they would have it, that locusts of every kind are entirely smooth and hairless. At least I find in Alcamus that قرن الجراد شعران في راسه [qarn al-jarād shaʿrān fī rāsih] is the name given to the horn of the locust, the two hairs which it has on its head ^{(3)}: and on account of these, why should it not be said to bristle or to stand on end when it raises them upright? So Aelian writes of the haemorrhous in History, book 15, chapter 13: Φρίττει δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν οἱονεὶ κέρασί τισιν [Phrittei de tēn kephalēn hoionei kerasi tisin]. Its head bristles as if with certain horns. Moreover, a poet of great name, Claudian, begins his description of the locust thus:
The crown of its head bristles, fierce eyes rise from the middle of its head, etc.
